title: Mercy asked for
hookLine: the prayer asks for mercy, not reward (Sukhmani 20)

cards: A loyalty card at a coffee shop. Ten stamps, and the eleventh cup is free. It's a tidy little deal: you do this, you get that.
A lot of life runs like that card, and a lot of religion is imagined that way too. Pray enough, give enough, behave well enough, and eventually the reward is stamped and due.
Sukhmani's twentieth ashtpadi tucks two small words into the beggar's request that tear the card in half. Kar kirpaa.

teach.b: Yesterday's stanza, in paraphrase: the beggar begs for a gift; in Your mercy, give me Your Name. Kar kirpaa: do mercy, show kindness.
Kirpaa is grace or mercy, a gift given because the giver is kind, not because the receiver has filled a card.

And the word for what's asked, daan, is a gift too: alms, charity. Nothing in that sentence is owed. Day five hundred met the same thread in Japji: actions shape a life, but grace, nadar, opens the gate.
Today it's in the beggar's own mouth. Deeds matter; Sikhs are expected to work, serve, and live well.

teach.h: ASKED AS A GIFT, NOT BOUGHT.
teach.b: But what the beggar asks for isn't bought by them. It's given, the way a gift is given. Why does that matter on an ordinary Tuesday?
Because how you think you're treated tends to become how you treat others. If everything is earned, then the people who've hurt you owe you, and the debt can feel permanent.

If you've been met with mercy, the ledger loosens. There's a salok of the poet-saint Kabir, recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib, that makes the link plainly. In paraphrase: where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.
Khimaa, forgiveness, is mercy turned outward.
The beggar who asks for kirpaa learns, slowly, to give some away.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twentieth ashtpadi ask for the Name with the words kar kirpaa, in Your mercy, and Gurbani links grace received with forgiveness given.

o: a reward paid for years of devotion
a fine paid to make up for a wrong
mercy or grace, given as a gift, not owed

games.q: mercy asked for — tap the pairs.
p: what loosens when mercy is met

s: the practice loosens the ledger without excusing what happened.
Kabir's salok in the Guru Granth Sahib links forgiveness with God
in paraphrase: where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.
the beggar asks for the Name as payment for devotion
kar kirpaa: in Your mercy. it's asked as a gift.

games.q: someone who hurt you in a small way says sorry. by today's lesson, what's the move?
o: make them earn it back, stamp by stamp.
offer a little more mercy than they've earned.
games.why: the beggar who is given mercy learns to give it. Kabir's salok puts it plainly: where there is forgiveness, there is God.

practice: Picture someone who hurt you in a small way, not the deepest wound, a friend who canceled, a driver who cut you off, a sibling's careless comment, and notice the ledger in your chest: they owe me.
On each breath out, loosen it a little; you don't have to excuse what happened, you're simply choosing not to keep stamping the card. If you pray, say Waheguru as you let go.

wordCard.voice: Kirpaa, mercy or grace: the beggar asks with kar kirpaa, in Your kirpaa, and the Name is given as a gift, not earned as a wage.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirpaa, mercy or grace; kar kirpaa, do mercy, opens many requests in Gurbani.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy, not reward. Nothing in the beggar's request is owed. Day five hundred sixteen, done.
